speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: The Bill introduces amendments to eight Acts, namely: (a) The Accountants Act 2004; (b) The Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority Act 2004; (c) The Business Names Registration Act 2014; (d) The Companies Act 1967; (e) The Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2005; (f) The Limited Partnerships Act 2008; (g) The Variable Capital Companies Act 2018; and (h) The Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: As the national business registry, ACRA maintains and makes publicly available information about business entities and their associated individuals, including their residential addresses, to facilitate regulatory and enforcement actions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: However, residential addresses can be exploited for malicious purposes, such as harassment and vice-related or loan shark activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: The contact address must be a physical address at which the individual can be reached or contacted by post, for instance, his or her office.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Individuals can still opt to use their residential addresses as their contact address, if they prefer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Should an individual be unreachable at the contact address, the Registrar is legally empowered to make the residential address public.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: The contact address regime differs from the existing alternate address regime in that: under the current alternate address regime, filing an alternate address is optional and individuals have to pay a fee to file an alternate address.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: With the introduction of the new contact address regime, the existing alternate address regime will be discontinued.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: To ease transition to the new contact address regime, existing alternate addresses will automatically convert to contact addresses upon the commencement of the amended Acts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: For those who have not filed an alternate address and wish to use a non-residential contact address, you can update your information with ACRA at no cost.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Corporate service providers should also verify their clients' preferred addresses and update ACRA accordingly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: As long as the alternate addresses are filed before commencement of the amended Acts, these will be reflected as contact addresses upon commencement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: If an alternate address is not filed by the time of the commencement of the amended Acts, the residential address will serve as the default contact address, with the option to update at any time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: The Bill also introduces a new framework for differentiated information disclosure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: This framework protects confidentiality of personal information by limiting public access, while still allowing selected, specified parties to access the information to fulfil their legal obligations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: For example, residential addresses will not be made publicly available by default.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: But certain parties, such as financial institutions, may still require the information to conduct customer due diligence checks on business entities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: The Bill allows specified parties to access selected personal information to fulfil their regulatory obligations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: These specified parties will be required to properly safeguard the use of such information.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: The second set of amendments aims to facilitate digital communications between the Government and businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Today, the Registrar still sends documents, not in connection with Court proceedings, in hard copy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Recipients will be notified via their provided email addresses to retrieve documents on their BizFile digital mailbox.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Hard copy documents will still be sent for Court proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: The third and final set of amendments seeks to enhance ACRA's regulatory oversight and streamline processes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: For instance, the Bill will allow the Registrar to obtain and use information from prescribed public agencies, reducing manual entry by users and enabling ACRA to maintain, rectify and update its registers more efficiently.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: This will provide greater convenience to individuals and entities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: In addition, the Bill will also allow the Registrar to use any information obtained from prescribed entities, such as electricity and telecommunication companies, to verify the accuracy of any document or information in ACRA's repository.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: This will support ACRA in performing its enforcement and regulatory functions, for instance, to detect businesses that are set up for illicit activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: These amendments will also enable ACRA to advance its regulatory framework, better protect data in its registry and facilitate data collection and usage for regulatory needs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the use of the BizFile+ digital mailbox to send statutory correspondence and notices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the public consultation, Ministry of Finance (MOF) and ACRA clarified that customers will be informed, including by email, when they receive new information or documents posted through the digital mailbox.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The timing of when documents are received may be important, especially in Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will it be based on when the document is posted in the digital mailbox, when the customer is informed about the posting, or when the customer accesses the documents in the digital mailbox?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOF and ACRA have also made clear that hard copy documents for Court proceedings will still be sent via registered post.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share if there are any plans to allow Court documents to be served via the digital mailbox?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, the Courts have now recognised substituted service of Court documents for civil proceedings via the Singpass app inbox.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, what factors will the Ministry consider in determining whether it is appropriate to allow service via the digital mailbox?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the ceasing the exclusion of residential addresses from public disclosure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, section 30C(1) prohibits any individual's residential address from being publicly disclosed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, section 30D(1) sets out two exceptions where an individual's residential address may cease to be excluded from public disclosure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This includes where communications sent require a response within a specified period or where service of any document at the individual's contact address is not effective to bring it to the notice of the individual.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, under section 30D(8), if the Registrar causes an individual's residential address to cease to be excluded from public disclosure, the individual will not be allowed to provide a contact address within three years unless the Registrar is satisfied that there is good cause to allow the individual to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify the rationale for not allowing the individual to provide a contact address within three years?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share what would be considered good cause to allow an individual to do so?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, when lawyers commence legal proceedings, they have to effect service on the individual personally and, sometimes, those persons are not at the office.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, when they cannot be found in the office, the lawyers will serve them at home based on the residential addresses listed in the ACRA corporate registers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify whether lawyers will still be able to obtain the residential addresses for the purposes of service of process?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point is on the provision of information and documents to third parties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under section 30B(1), ACRA may provide information and documents to certain third parties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These third parties include authorised information service providers, trustees of a bankrupt's estate, liquidators, judicial managers, receivers, financial institutions, moneylenders and estate agents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Once the information is provided to these third parties, the information is then subject to the third party's data protection and management policies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My concern is that the capabilities around protecting data may vary across different third parties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, a moneylender or a real estate agent may not be able to set up data protection as robust as those of a financial institution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is noteworthy because the information ACRA shares may include personal data.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, will ACRA require an undertaking from these third parties on the use and protection of the information provided?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I support the Bill but will flag some areas of concern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will begin by discussing the two main thrusts of the Bill pertaining to improving the business environment and enhancing corporate regulation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will then move on to some more general reflections on the fundamental tensions between these two objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since much of the Bill pertains to the business climate, I will also state at the outset that I am an associate professor at a business school.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By a similar token, expanding the recognition of financial statements prepared according to internationally accepted standards, as embodied in clause 48, will make it easier for foreign investors to register the subsidiaries of their businesses locally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Further simplifying the procedures involved in setting up private enterprises, not least by making the different arms of the Government talk to one another, will continue to lighten the burden of regulation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This, in turn, has the potential to spur further entrepreneurial activity, promote competition, stimulate the growth of existing businesses and even, potentially, raise productivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, Singapore already does reasonably well by this standard.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is a reminder that other economies do not sit still, even as we strive to continue to improve our own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, any steps that we can take to continue easing the process of new business formation should, in and of itself, be welcome.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the amendments also enfold certain rudimentary personal data protections, especially pertaining to residential addresses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Several clauses apply the same to related acts, such as clause 14 for public accountants to list a distinct contact address for public inspection in the Accountants Act, or clause 40 for directors, chief executives or secretaries in the Companies Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These basic protections are to be welcome, not least, because in an age of pervasive information dissemination, where, as we all know, the Internet never forgets, individuals and their families should, at least, be able to find some refuge from public scrutiny in their homes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This naturally begs the question of whether providing information that differs from official residency information may inhibit Police or judicial operations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Certain clauses, such as clauses 19, 26 and 45, stipulate that documents may be directly served to contact addresses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will note that clause 26 specifically states that such documents may be sent either via ordinary or prepaid registered post, but notably, no such language is included in clauses 19, 34, 45 or 65, albeit the preamble definition of contact address, which indicates the necessity of a physical address at which the individual can be contacted by post, may be sufficient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relatedly, it does strike me as somewhat odd that there is no requirement that registered post be used to ensure receipt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is a fairly common practice for at least initial attempts at personal service prior to any application for substituted service thereafter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Clause 39 allows the registrar to unilaterally amend the register of directors for a company with reasonable cause.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But when paired with clause 8, where information may be obtained from any authorised information service provider, which could, of course, entail non-governmental entities, problems could emerge, especially in a world where there may be incentives to generate fraudulent information, or even if, in the absence of malicious intent, such entities suffer from lapses that could corrupt their databases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be fair, the proposed amendments to section 30A, Part 4, relieves the person of liability if there is erroneous or inaccurate information collected, if they have not been offered an opportunity to verify the said information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it nonetheless raises questions about how much the Government should be reliant on external information sources.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will be the first to acknowledge that restricting data providers to only intra-Government sources may be even worse, given capacity limitations in the public sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it, nevertheless, places a strong onus on the Government to carefully verify the accuracy of information obtained.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I trust that this will be emphasised to public officials as part of standard operating procedures as they will go about their due diligence processes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, I hope that ACRA will clearly post information on its website that explains the appeal mechanisms that may be available to individuals who wish to contest a disqualification.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In this sense, then, it is important to remember that we must guard against carrying any pro-business policy too far.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We must understand that supporting business does not imply coddling them from exposure to competitive market forces nor does it preclude taking care of other stakeholders, especially workers, in our economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For these reasons, sensible regulation must be necessary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Recent events surrounding the Doing Business report are instructive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Worse, the indicators were accused of favouring a right-leaning ideology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, it included an indicator for paying taxes that seemed to suggest that lower corporate taxes were always unambiguously better.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As the Workers' Party has argued on multiple occasions in this House before, a higher effective corporate tax rate, if directed appropriately, can yield many positive benefits, ranging from averting an increase in the Goods and Services Tax (GST) to providing further relief to small and medium enterprises (SMEs), to reinvesting more in our home-grown companies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another controversial indicator related to employing workers, where more robust labour regulations were treated crudely as a cost, thereby failing to take into account the offsetting benefits of stronger employment protections.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The indicator was justifiably excluded from the compilation of the Aggregate Index since 2011, but its presence in the report was, nevertheless, viewed as symptomatic of the report's implicit biases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More generally, we should also not allow the world to think that an easy business environment also means a permissive one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some have even suggested the term "Singapore-washing", the process where foreign actors take advantage of our relatively simple registration processes and global reputation for incorruptibility to incorporate fronts for dubious business activities, in some form of a quid pro quo for investing in our city-state.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such a mindset will undermine our very hard-won brand name and eventually come back to bite us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Recent incidents have already raised questions on how indulgent we appear to be of illicit activities, especially with regard to financial flows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, US court documents revealed that the companies he registered here were shell companies used to "concealed the identity and illegitimate nature of his proceeds".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am aware that we will be debating the Anti-Money Laundering Bill in this House next month, where these matters are very likely to be debated at length.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nevertheless, I hope that we will reflect on whether our drive towards simplifying doing business here may have ended up erring on the side of becoming too permissive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In closing, I will urge this House to guard against allowing the undeniable benefits of a favourable business climate to entrench itself as an ideology, divorced from the counter-balancing role of sound corporate regulation and, subsequently, insulated from critique.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Internal criticism of the Doing Business report contributed to the resignation of the then-Chief Economist of the World Bank.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As we debate the present Bill in Parliament, it is my hope that we also remain clear-eyed on the value of considered, constructive criticism of our own business environment, too.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   The first set of queries relate to the purpose of the Bill and its impact on businesses.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will the use of a digital mailbox for statutory correspondences and notices (excluding summons) will affect the communication process for businesses and individuals?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would also like to know which specific Government agencies will provide information to ACRA to keep its registers up to date.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, how will the process of updating registers with information from these agencies be managed and monitored for accuracy?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Government agencies like the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) and the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) should have the most updated information.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My second set of questions concern foreign companies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will these changes benefit foreign companies operating in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One of the proposed changes is to empower the Registrar to notify the recipient via electronic means on how and when to access documents and information sent by the Registrar.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How does the Registrar verify or ensure that the foreign recipients' email addresses or mobile numbers belong to the rightful person?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Foreign companies incorporated by the same corporate secretaries may already be sharing the same email addresses or office numbers when updating their particulars with ACRA. : Thirdly, on data privacy and security.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What measures will be in place to protect the data in the digital mailboxes?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, what are the new powers granted to the Registrar concerning the registers of directors?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will the Registrar determine and reflect the disqualification status of the individuals?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Ministry share with the House what were the main concerns and feedback raised during public consultation?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How have MOF or ACRA addressed these concerns in the final version of the Bill?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding my queries, I can see the many benefits from these amendments.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can expect enhanced efficiency and speed in communication between ACRA and business entities, potential cost savings by reducing physical mail and increased accountability for businesses to maintain updated contact information.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With more accurate and up-to-date registers, the administrative burden on businesses should be reduced.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Compliance processes may be simplified due to better integration with other Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There should also be greater privacy and security with improved data protection through a tiered disclosure framework, through businesses that may need to invest to meet new data security requirements.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As the Registrar will be better empowered to maintain accurate records of directors, including disqualification status, this could lead to greater transparency and trust in corporate governance.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For foreign companies, these changes would potentially reduce compliance costs and administrative burdens, too, making Singapore a more attractive destination for their investments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, the new regulations must ensure digital inclusion and smooth implementation for all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill mandates the use of electronic transaction systems for interactions with the Registrar.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, we must also consider the potential accessibility issues that may arise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are individuals and small business owners who may lack digital literacy or access to reliable Internet services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The digital divide is a reality we must acknowledge and address.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is our responsibility to ensure that the benefits of digitalisation are accessible to all, regardless of their digital literacy or Internet accessibility, and that no one is left behind.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must consider and mitigate any negative impact on SMEs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: SMEs are the backbone of our economy, providing employment, fostering innovation and contributing significantly to our gross domestic product (GDP).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, for any regulatory changes, we must consider the potential impacts on these vital entities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Specifically, these businesses may lack the resources to quickly adapt to new regulations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The costs of compliance can also be disproportionately higher for them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need policies that support, rather than hinder these businesses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: An effective way to address the concerns of businesses and render the necessary support, is clear implementation and transition periods.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will give stakeholders time and resources to adapt.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A clear and manageable transition plan is critical to ensure that stakeholders are adequately prepared for the changes, reducing potential disruptions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to understand how these changes will be rolled out and over what time period.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, what support mechanisms are in place for entities to transition smoothly to these requirements?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, this Bill must address data privacy concerns, while ensuring alignment with international standards.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill provides for the sharing of information, including personal data, with authorised information service providers and other public agencies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is a matter of great significance, especially in an era where data breaches are increasingly common and global concerns about data privacy are at an all-time high.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this data age, data is an asset, but it can also be a liability if not handled with the utmost care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure that the Bill aligns with the best practices in data security.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need robust data protection measures that not only comply with our national standards but also stand up to international scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we strive to enhance our corporate regulatory regime and data management practices, it is critical that we benchmark ourselves against the best in the world.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there specific countries or frameworks that influenced the drafting of this Bill?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Understanding this can provide valuable insights into the strengths of our Bill and areas where we can improve.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It can also help us ensure that Singapore remains competitive and compliant with international norms.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Further to the above, I am heartened by the exclusion of residential address from public disclosure, if contact address is available, pursuant to the proposed new section 30C.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In particular, the new provisions would prevent the misuse of the residential address of company officers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such misuse may include the use of such residential address for the purposes of harassing officers for perceived wrongs of the company.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, we must commit to a process of continuous monitoring and evaluation to ensure the long-term effectiveness and impact of the changes introduced by this Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister explain the mechanisms that will be put in place to monitor and evaluate the long-term effectiveness and impact of these changes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need robust systems that allow us to track the outcomes of our legislation and make necessary adjustments over time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, how will the Ministry ensure that the Bill's objectives are being met without unintended negative consequences?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Legislation, no matter how well-intended, can sometimes have unforeseen impacts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is our responsibility to monitor these impacts and take corrective actions when necessary.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Continuous monitoring and evaluation are essential for adapting and improving regulatory frameworks over time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Both pieces of legislation aim to enhance our audit regulatory regime and introduce measures for better compliance with professional requirements and standards.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is a testament to our continuous efforts to strengthen our regulatory framework and maintain the highest standards of corporate governance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As someone who is not an accountant by training, but who has studied financial markets and econometrics, and works in an international investment firm, I view these changes as necessary and important from a private sector perspective.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, as mentioned above, I urge the Ministry to consider the following.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure a smooth transition for all stakeholders, including those with limited digital literacy or Internet access.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need a plan to monitor and evaluate the long-term impact of these changes to ensure that they achieve their objectives without unintended consequences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore is an established international financial centre and we aspire to project ourselves further, to be a leading global financial centre in the world.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill will tighten and enhance our measures vis a vis corporate governance, which will hopefully minimise such cases moving forward.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In doing so, we will improve investor confidence in Singapore, in a world now increasingly fraught with uncertainty, especially with digitalisation and cybercrimes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ensuring that our information collected is updated is a critical part of this process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us ensure that Singapore remains a competitive and compliant global financial centre through this digital transformation, but also one that is inclusive and protects data privacy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They have raised questions around four main themes, which can be summarised as follows: one, relating to the transition to digital communications; two, the introduction of the new contact address regime; three, data protection and information sharing; and four, the proposed enhancements to the corporate regulatory regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how documents sent digitally would be deemed to have been received by the recipient.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Don Wee asked about the security of ACRA's digital mailbox system and how the Registrar can ensure that the email addresses provided are accurate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As the email notification serves to alert individuals and businesses to access the information or documents addressed to them or their associated business entities, it is in the recipient's interests and their responsibility to provide an accurate email address to ACRA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If, for example, they do not fulfil their obligations under the Companies Act because they had provided an inaccurate or outdated email address and did not receive the alerts on ACRA's reminders and notices, they can still be held responsible.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To Mr Don Wee's query on security, the BizFile system is a secure environment and any information or document uploaded to the digital mailbox can only be accessed by individuals and businesses when they log in with their Singpass and/or CorpPass.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether there are any plans to allow Court documents to be served digitally.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: While the Bill does not cover that, ACRA will consider Mr Louis Ng's suggestion in future reviews but that will also depend on the rules of Court and what they permit.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Don Wee and Mr Yip Hon Weng also asked about the impact of the transition to digital communications on individuals and businesses, particularly SMEs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Given that digital filing has been in place since 2003, most individuals and businesses that transact with ACRA would be familiar with the BizFile portal.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we expect the transition to digital communications to be manageable.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: During this time, ACRA will send both hard copy documents and digital copies with reminders about the full transition to digital communications.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, I will address questions relating to the contact address regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how the disclosure of residential addresses when the contact address is found to be not effective will help to bring documents to the individual's notice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As mentioned in my opening speech, the contact and residential addresses are key in reaching individuals associated with the company.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the individual cannot be reached at the contact address provided, it would not be unreasonable to assume that the contact address is either inaccurate or outdated.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To ensure that the individual can still be reached, ACRA may then disclose the individual's residential address for corporate transparency and to allow effective service of documents because, presumably, the individual will have to go home at some point in time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked about the rationale for imposing a three-year restriction on updating contact addresses after the residential address is disclosed by the Registrar.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We do not want individuals to intentionally file inaccurate contact addresses in order to avoid being reached, which would undermine the contact address regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, if individuals are uncontactable at the contact addresses they provided, it suggests these addresses are ineffective as a way to reach these individuals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this situation, ACRA has the power to publicly disclose their residential addresses for corporate transparency purposes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Once this happens, then, as a form of deterrence, these individuals will not be allowed to put up new contact addresses for a period of three years, even if they wish to do so for privacy reasons.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They will have to accept their residential address functioning as the contact address for three years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, if an individual genuinely needs the three-year restriction to be reviewed, they can make an application to the Registrar, who will consider the facts and circumstances of each case before deciding whether to allow the individual to provide another contact address.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether lawyers will be able to obtain residential addresses of individuals registered with ACRA for the purpose of service of Court processes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The scope of the Bill does not presently cover this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, the Member has raised a good suggestion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng, Mr Don Wee and Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the safeguards in place when sharing information with authorised information service providers and other specified persons.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: ACRA will implement the necessary safeguards, which include requiring these third parties to sign undertakings or agree to terms and conditions governing data use to prevent the disclosure of data to unauthorised persons or for unauthorised purposes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Don Wee asked which Government agencies would provide information to ACRA and the accuracy of such information.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For instance, the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority, or ICA, will provide realtime data updates of NRIC holders' personal information to ACRA registers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If any data discrepancies come to ACRA's attention, ACRA will conduct verification with the relevant agencies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This ensures accuracy of ACRA's registers and provides greater convenience to individuals and businesses who do not then need to update multiple agencies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Fourth, let me address questions related to the refinements to our corporate regulatory regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Don Wee asked about the Registrar's powers in relation to the registers of directors and how the Registrar will determine and reflect the disqualification status of disqualified directors on ACRA registers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This status will be publicly accessible, ensuring transparency on the eligibility of individuals to be appointed as directors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Once the disqualification period ends, the status will be removed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Don Wee also asked about the changes to the financial reporting requirements for foreign companies registered under the Companies Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, if a foreign company is listed in Singapore overseas, it can lodge with ACRA the financial statements prepared in compliance with the applicable rules of the exchange on which it is listed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In relation to the questions raised by Members on the Bill process, let me assure the House that careful study has been done in the formulation of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We looked at the best practices of leading jurisdictions and adopted them for our local context.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, our approach to not disclose residential addresses of individuals associated with businesses is similar to the United Kingdom and Hong Kong.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the public consultations held in 2020, 2022 and 2024, the feedback received was broadly in support of the proposals and we incorporated the relevant feedback received into this Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, financial institutions highlighted the need to have access to residential addresses of individuals associated with businesses for compliance with anti-money laundering statutory obligations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As I have mentioned in my earlier speech, we accepted this feedback and provided for this under the disclosure framework.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also regularly review our policies and legislation to maintain a pro-business environment while ensuring a robust regulatory regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim had a couple of questions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He had mentioned, in relation to foreign companies, the suggestion was that clause 48 would make it easier for foreign investors to register the subsidiaries of their businesses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I just want to clarify that the purpose of clause 48 is not to make it easier for foreign investors to register their companies, but as I mentioned in my speech earlier, it relates to the streamlining of financial reporting requirements by foreign companies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, if they have already prepared financial statements which substantially meet our requirements, then they can use that and it is easier for them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There was another point which Assoc Prof Jamus Lim raised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He mentioned that it is odd that there was no requirement that registered posts be used to ensure receipt, it being a common practice for, at least, initial attempts at personal service prior to any application for substituted service thereafter.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim may be confused between the three.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Registered post is not the same as personal service and personal service is not the same as substituted service.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When there is personal service, you have to actually hand it to the person directly, in person.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You would never, in any circumstances, use registered post as a means for personal service, nor would it be a prerequisite.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You would send by way of registered post if you want to be doubly sure that it reaches a certain address.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But registered post does not ensure it reaches an individual because you can have registered post delivered to a certain address.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The domestic helper may be at home, another family member may be at home, not the addressee.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So long as they receive it and sign for it, it is registered, but that is not personal service.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, substituted service comes when you are not able to actually deliver to the person face-to-face.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Usually, for Court documents, the Court is satisfied that you could not meet that person face-to-face, so you have a substituted service, leaving it at the doorstep, in some cases, if the Court allows, sending it digitally.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, I just wanted to lay that framework so that everybody understands all three are very separate things for separate purposes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, in terms of what the regime provides, first, documents for Court proceedings will continue to be served in hard copy, including whichever means they are required to be served.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There was one more question, which was whether the contact address would inhibit Police or enforcement action.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is just that they will not be made public, but ACRA can share the residential address and other data or information with other Government agencies if needed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With that, Sir, in conclusion, the amendments in this Bill will strengthen data protection, facilitate digital communications between the Government and businesses and streamline our corporate regulatory framework.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It strikes a fine balance between corporate transparency and personal data protection as we advance the digitalisation of our corporate regulatory services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In fact, my comment is a little more straightforward and, that is, that in one of the clauses, clause 26, it states specifically that documents may be sent by ordinary or prepaid registered post.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But for clauses 19, 34, 45 and 65, in terms of contacting the individual, no such requirement exists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I thought that there was an inconsistency that I hope the Minister will be able to clarify.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Which were the other clauses that were being referred to?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Yes, they were clauses 19, 34, 45 and 65.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the Act sometimes prescribes situations where a specific mode has to be followed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But when you file general particulars, there is a general address.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Clause 16, if I am not mistaken and that was the one that was being referred to— no, clause 19, that talks about the alternate address being replaced with contact address.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: An alternate address is one of those generic addresses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, when you print out the search in an ACRA search, you will see director's name.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is the generic one and this is the one for alternate addresses which will be replaced by the contact address regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Clearly, in the Act, it contemplates different underlying functions, and you have different addresses or different things for that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, one refers to the address, the other refers to the mode of delivery of the document.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 4.33 pm until 4.50 pm.
